name: King's Gambit
subtitle: Trade a pawn for the initiative.

ideas.idea: Offer the f-pawn to pull Black's central pawn away from the centre. Your compensation is time: build a broad centre, develop with threats, and make the open f-file useful before Black can consolidate. The sacrifice is a practical invitation to an unbalanced fight, not a promise of an advantage.
ideas.structure: The e- and d-pawns can claim central space, but advancing them carelessly leaves squares behind. Black's extra pawn on the f-file can restrict your pieces or become a target. If Black supports it with king-side pawns, look at the squares those pawns have stopped defending before deciding to break the chain.
ideas.pieces: A knight often belongs on f3, both developing and reducing checks on the queen's diagonal. The light-squared bishop looks toward f7, and castling can bring a rook to the open file. Finish mobilizing your queen-side pieces rather than expecting two attackers to do all the work.
ideas.motifs: Watch the diagonal leading to h4: moving the f-pawn has weakened your own king. Pressure on f7, discoveries along the f-file, and attacks on a stretched pawn chain are recurring themes. A flashy sacrifice on f7 needs a concrete calculation, not just a familiar pattern.
ideas.declined: If Black develops a bishop instead of taking, claim the centre without assuming you have won a free tempo. A central counterstrike asks a different question: resolve the central tension and watch for an advanced enemy e-pawn that can gain time against your pieces.
ideas.caution: Your king is part of the price. If the attack stalls, stop chasing the pawn and improve king safety. Black can defend accurately and retain a sound position.

modelGames.summary: White never wins the f4 pawn back by force. Instead he undermines it, swaps into a queenless middlegame and shows that the lasting assets of the gambit—a strong centre and loose black pawns—still count when the attack is gone.

moments.title: A patient retreat
moments.note: Rather than sacrifice the knight, White simply steps back. Black has grabbed space with g5–g4, but those advanced pawns are now targets, and White still owns the centre with e4 and d4.

moments.title: Undermine, then recapture
moments.note: g3 forced the issue: the f4 pawn disappeared and a knight landed on g3. Material is level again, but White develops with gain of time while Black's kingside is full of holes.

moments.title: Queens off, edge stays
moments.note: Trading queens did not end White's pressure. Without queens the king is safe on d2, and the open e- and f-files plus Black's stranded g4 pawn still favour the gambit side.

moments.title: A rook on the sixth
moments.note: After the exchange on e6, White's rook lands deep in Black's camp. The pressure comes from activity, not a mating attack—exactly the kind of edge a well-played gambit leaves behind.

moments.title: The queenside harvest
moments.note: Black's pieces drifted to the kingside, and the knight quietly collects queenside pawns. Converting an initiative often means switching targets once the defender overreacts.

moments.title: Passed pawns decide
moments.note: The central pawns that White kept since the opening now roll forward together. The gambit's early centre has turned into a winning endgame asset.

modelGames.summary: White goes all-in with a knight sacrifice on f7 and later a rook. Black takes what is offered, brings the king back to safety and counterattacks on the h-file. A lesson in how a gambit fails when the extra sacrifices do not create concrete threats.

moments.title: Doubling the stakes
moments.note: White gives a whole knight to pull Black's king into the open. Sacrifices like this only work if the attack lands quickly; otherwise Black is simply a piece up.

moments.title: Counterattack beats passivity
moments.note: Instead of only defending, Black's queen grabs the h-pawn and starts eyeing White's king. Every tempo White spends parrying threats is a tempo not spent attacking.

moments.title: Take it and hold on
moments.note: White threw in a rook on f7 as well. Black captures it: the king looks exposed, but White has too few pieces left to exploit it, and every trade now favours the defender.

moments.title: Giving back to kill the attack
moments.note: Black returns the exchange on f2. When you are far ahead in material, giving some back to remove the attacker's best piece is a classic way to finish the defence.

moments.title: The hunter becomes the hunted
moments.note: The g-pawn hits White's queen and opens the road to h2. White's king, not Black's, is now the one facing mate.
